sentences.text: The genus Deltadromeus contains only one known species, D. agilis, known from an incomplete postcranial skeleton.
Based on the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — this animal was approximately 8 meters long and weighed 1050 kilograms.
It possessed relatively long forelimbs, which were proportionately longer than those of Allosaurus.
The tail vertebrae featured broad, quadrangular neural spines with pleurocoels, internal cavities that likely stored pneumatic air sacs.
American paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues formally described the genus Deltadromeus in 1996.
Fossils definitively assigned to this genus were discovered that same year by Sereno during an expedition in the Kem Kem Beds of eastern Morocco.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as SGM-Din 2, was an incomplete postcranial skeleton found at a single site.
Isotopic evidence suggests carcharodontosaurids and ceratosaurs in the Kem Kem Beds and Elrhaz Formation consumed sizable terrestrial animals.
Researchers suggest niche partitioning occurred among theropods, with spinosaurids eating fish and other groups hunting herbivorous dinosaurs.
If Deltadromeus is closely related to herbivorous or omnivorous ceratosaurs like Limusaurus, it may have been herbivorous or omnivorous.
Abelisauroid affinities suggest Deltadromeus may have been omnivorous or herbivorous.
Originally classified as a basal coelurosaur related to Ornitholestes, this classification has been challenged by later studies.
Some studies have classified Deltadromeus as an avetheropod related to Gualicho or as a megaraptoran outside the family Megaraptoridae.
Other researchers propose Deltadromeus is a ceratosaur, but its exact position within Ceratosauria remains debated.
The dinosaur has been classified variously as a basal ceratosaur, a noasaurid, or an Elaphrosaurus-grade ceratosaur.
Fossils of Deltadromeus date to the Cenomanian stage of the Cretaceous period, approximately 100 to 95 million years ago.
Remains are found in the Kem Kem Beds of North Africa, as well as the Bahariya Formation of Egypt and the Elrhaz and Echkar Formations of Niger.
During the Cretaceous, North Africa was covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, supporting diverse fish, crocodyliforms, and pterosaurs.

It is debated whether Deltadromeus and Bahariasaurus are distinct genera or if one is a synonym of the other, with some studies suggesting Deltadromeus may be a junior synonym of Bahariasaurus, though this is not universally accepted.
Researchers cannot yet confirm if certain teeth belong to Deltadromeus due to a lack of fossil overlap and ongoing controversy about its classification.
